sib.t: David Wakeling — A&O Shearman (Global Head of AI)

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Wakeling does not assess the cluster’s central claims about jagged task capability, user expertise, verification or work redesign. He instead reframes the deployment bottleneck as fragmented cross-jurisdictional regulation and prioritises iterative global standard-setting, harmonisation and mutual recognition to give deployers practical certainty.

st.t: Deployment controls: Useful AI needs proportionate safeguards
st.an: Wakeling accepts the need for workable safeguards that permit useful AI deployment and materially develops the proposition by proposing an internationally coordinated framework, detailed standards, aligned timetables and mutual recognition. He also advocates iterative revision as evidence emerges, while acknowledging that jurisdictional competition obstructs coordination.

kp.k: Firm-wide deployment and software-mediated legal advice
kp.d: Wakeling reports that the firm deployed generative AI in December 22 across 4,000 lawyers and 43 jurisdictions, claiming it was the first law firm to do so across its business. He says Contract Matrix, built with Microsoft and Harvey the previous year, was designed to accelerate contract drafting and negotiation and introduce a business model delivering legal advice through AI software. These are practitioner-reported deployment and product claims, not measured productivity findings.
qs: in December 22 we became the first law firm to deploy generative AI across our business that meant 4,000 lawyers and it meant 43 jurisdictions
that was designed to speed up contract Drafting and contract negotiation
we built that in partnership with Microsoft and Harvey and we created a new business model for lawyers the idea being could deliver legal advice to clients via AI software

kp.k: Fragmented principles leave deployers without operational clarity
kp.d: From the perspective of a law-firm deployer and adviser to business clients, Wakeling argues that proliferating international and national AI initiatives offer similar but nonidentical abstract principles. He says businesses are already deploying AI at a level of detail these frameworks do not address, while even binding legislation leaves substantial interpretive uncertainty.
qs: it's leading to a kind of Patchwork of mostly voluntary principles at least for the moment
each organization publishing is approaching it in a slightly different way and it's starting to feel like a lofty Echo chamber
even binding legislation leaves Acres of interpretation
businesses are guessing the detail they're making decisions blind

kp.k: Regulatory ambiguity makes legal guidance costly and slow
kp.d: Wakeling describes running a client working group to interpret the EU AI Act's practical implications. Deployers turn to lawyers to identify risks and determine acceptable deployment practices, but he characterizes this individualized interpretation as expensive and slow. He reports that uncertainty discourages use cases and entry into jurisdictions rather than merely increasing compliance work.
qs: I run an AI working group of clients like a Syndicate of clients
deployers come to their lawyers to help them decide what good looks like
it's very expensive very slow process
businesses are choosing not to pursue certain use cases because it's too hard

kp.k: Compliance concerns constrained the firm's own deployment
kp.d: As concrete examples, Wakeling reports that after considering rules in over 40 jurisdictions, the firm excluded generative AI from every HR function globally and declined deployment in two unnamed G20 jurisdictions. He attributes one country exclusion to regulatory uncertainty and the other to complex rules layered with data-localization requirements. These examples describe the firm's decisions rather than general adoption statistics.

we decided not to deploy any generative Ai and any HR function in the world

because it was so unclear as a regulat environment we just gave up

kp.k: Uncertainty risks regulatory arbitrage and consumer harm
kp.d: Wakeling argues that unclear or hastily constructed rules and insufficiently informed voluntary codes create divergent deployment practices. He identifies regulatory arbitrage as a possible consequence, arguing that compliance-conscious businesses face innovation barriers while bad actors retain opportunities and consumers may encounter poorly informed deployment decisions. These are asserted mechanisms and risks, not quantified findings.

kp.k: Banking reforms provide an analogy for coordinated AI governance
kp.d: Drawing on his legal experience with the global banking crisis and LIBOR reform, Wakeling recommends a single globally supported, high-level AI framework followed by detailed regulator-level coordination. He presents banking reforms as precedent for developing a common global baseline while respecting national laws and legislative processes, not as evidence that equivalent AI coordination has already occurred.

kp.k: Common timetables and consultation support workable standards
kp.d: Wakeling describes synchronized implementation and extensive industry–regulator collaboration in banking reform as mechanisms for limiting jurisdiction shopping and producing precise standards. He recommends comparable coordination for AI, supported by iterative consultation with market participants, trade associations and other stakeholders, including attention to vulnerable groups.

kp.k: Mutual recognition could reduce duplicated compliance
kp.d: Wakeling proposes mutual recognition as an aspirational outcome of sufficiently detailed regulatory harmonization: compliance in one jurisdiction would satisfy requirements in another without a second round of checking. He emphasizes that this depends on substantial regulator-level work and multistakeholder consensus, and identifies Partnership on AI as a forum that can help develop such standards and agreement.

it's a hugely aspirational thing to do

providing a forum for all the stakeholders industry Regulators governments po policy makers civil rights groups to try and build that consensus

kp.k: National AI competition obstructs global regulatory collaboration
kp.d: Asked why AI has not seen comparable detailed regulatory engagement, Wakeling identifies competition among jurisdictions to build domestic AI industries and secure economic growth as the largest obstacle. His hope that forthcoming forums will reduce this barrier is prospective; he says the absence of a settled global framework makes detailed coordination harder.

everyone's thinking I'm going to make my own AI industry this is economic growth
I would say that's the biggest single obstacle
it's very hard to get into level below if that one isn't pinned down

kp.k: Incomplete understanding calls for iterative regulation
kp.d: An audience member questions whether AI's technical opacity limits the banking analogy. Wakeling responds that banking policymakers also initially lacked impact data, arguing for proceeding with principles, standards and detail while continuously improving rules as effects become visible. This is his response to uncertainty, not a finding that AI and banking present identical regulatory problems.
qs: at the time of the banking crisis people didn't actually know the impact actually the data wasn't there that happened after
go with principles go with standards get into the detail but then they did continuous Improvement afterwards
they're still tweaking rules today that they set 10 years ago because they didn't get it fully right the first time

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Wakeling describes firm-wide generative AI deployment and an AI-software channel for delivering legal advice, alongside a broad expectation of disruption to law.
pts.d: Wakeling says his firm was the first law firm to deploy generative AI across its business, covering 4,000 lawyers and 43 jurisdictions, and subsequently the first to build an AI tool for lawyers, Contract Matrix, with Microsoft and Harvey. He describes faster contract drafting and negotiation as the tool's design objective, not a measured result, and presents delivering legal advice through AI software as a new business model. He also reports that law is widely regarded as among the five sectors most exposed to AI disruption, without specifying employment effects or the mechanism or magnitude of that disruption.

pts.k: Wakeling argues that fragmented and ambiguous AI regulation makes deployment dependent on expensive, slow legal interpretation and causes businesses to abandon uses and jurisdictions.
pts.d: He describes businesses already deploying AI while policy frameworks remain abstract and binding legislation still requires extensive interpretation. Lawyers consequently help clients determine acceptable deployment and manage customer and regulatory risks. He says this process is costly and slow and can deter deployment altogether. As concrete examples, he reports that his own firm excluded generative AI from HR globally and did not deploy in two unnamed G20 jurisdictions: one because the regulatory environment was unclear, the other because of complex rules layered onto data-localization requirements. His initial description of deployment across the business therefore should not be read as unrestricted deployment in every function or country.

pts.k: Wakeling says regulatory fragmentation can encourage jurisdiction shopping, inhibit responsible innovation and expose consumers to poor deployment decisions.
pts.d: His argument extends beyond legal services to business-to-business AI deployment generally. He links unclear or inadequately informed regulation to uncertainty and divergent practices, and says companies can seek easier jurisdictions for deployment. He identifies competition between countries to develop their own AI industries as the largest obstacle to the international cooperation he advocates. These are his causal assessments, not quantified findings.

pts.k: Wakeling proposes coordinated AI standards and eventual mutual recognition as a route to clearer, less duplicative cross-border compliance.
pts.d: He advocates a globally supported high-level framework, detailed regulator-led standards, a common implementation timetable and stakeholder feedback. He argues by analogy with banking reforms that sufficiently harmonized rules could permit compliance in one jurisdiction to count in another, avoiding a second compliance check. This is an aspirational proposal for AI, not a claim that AI mutual recognition already exists. He maintains that incomplete understanding need not prevent initial standards if they are continuously improved.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is principally Wakeling's first-hand deployment and client-advisory experience, supplemented by analogies to financial regulatory coordination.
pts.d: He grounds the operational claims in his role as head of AI, the reported deployment scale, the Contract Matrix partnership, his client working group and three internal deployment restrictions. He does not supply drafting-speed benchmarks, cost measurements, adoption outcomes or supporting research for the top-five disruption assertion. The anticipated benefits of regulatory coordination draw on his personal legal experience of post-financial-crisis reform and LIBOR transition, including coordinated timetables, consultations and mutual recognition. These banking examples are analogical support rather than observed AI-policy outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Deployment and compliance burdens are presented as current in the 2024 talk; broader disruption and regulatory convergence have no firm forecast date.
pts.d: Wakeling dates the initial deployment to December 2022 and describes Contract Matrix as built 'last year,' implying 2023 relative to the document's 2024 date. His claims about legal interpretation costs and abandoned deployments concern decisions already being made. He qualifies the policy patchwork as mostly voluntary 'at least for the moment' and acknowledges that some rules are clear. He hopes forthcoming forums will improve cooperation within the next few months but does not promise agreement. Mutual recognition depends on detailed harmonization, stakeholder consensus and coordinated implementation; rules would require revision as impacts become clearer.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are multinational law firms and their lawyers, corporate AI deployers and clients, with downstream consequences for consumers and regulators.
pts.d: For his firm and its lawyers, AI entails broad tool deployment, a contract-work application and a proposed software-mediated advice model, constrained by jurisdictional and functional exclusions. Corporate clients require legal help interpreting deployment obligations and may forgo uses or markets because of uncertainty and compliance effort. Responsible deployers face innovation barriers, while less responsible actors may exploit regulatory differences. Consumers may suffer from poorly judged deployment. Regulators, governments, industry and civil-rights stakeholders are the intended participants in coordinated standard-setting. Wakeling does not make specific claims about junior-lawyer displacement, staffing leverage, billing changes or access to justice.
